HIST 270 · Chapter 5 · Lecture 2

Early Tang Power

How did Tang rulers turn Sui foundations into a durable, expanding empire?

618Li Yuan founds the Tang
626Li Shimin seizes the throne
630Eastern Türk qaghanate collapses
645–676Korean campaigns reveal limits

Welcome to Lecture 2 of Chapter 5. You are moving from the Sui, which reunited China but collapsed under the weight of its demands, to the early Tang, which inherited many Sui institutions and made them last. The four dates give you the lecture’s backbone. Li Yuan founded the Tang in 618, but the new dynasty still had to defeat rivals across China. In 626 his son Li Shimin seized power and became Emperor Taizong. In 630 Tang forces destroyed the Eastern Türk qaghanate and Taizong accepted a steppe title as well as his Chinese imperial title. From 645 to 676, wars in and around the Korean peninsula showed that conquest and durable control were not the same thing.

Use the dotted phrases to open short explanations and the S key to open these Study Buddy notes. The self-check slides let you test yourself before reading the answer. Keep one question in mind: did early Tang strength come mainly from better institutions, better rulers, or better management of allies?

Check yourself: Which event on the timeline concerns succession inside the Tang family, and which two concern Tang relations beyond China’s agrarian heartland?

The historical problem

The Tang did not start over; it made inherited systems work together.

Consolidate

Defeat rivals and manage a violent succession.

Connect

Link registered households to land, taxes, law, and service.

Extend

Use armies, allies, titles, and local rulers beyond the core.

Argument: early Tang power rested on coordination. Its greatest victories combined institutions with relationships; its failures came when victory could not be converted into lasting cooperation.

This slide gives you the lecture’s argument. The early Tang became powerful by coordinating three tasks. First, the dynasty had to consolidate: Tang rulers defeated rival regimes and managed a dangerous struggle inside the ruling family. Second, they had to connect: household registers, land assignments, taxes, military service, law, and official recruitment worked as parts of one system. Third, they tried to extend power beyond the agrarian heartland through field armies, steppe allies, Chinese titles for local leaders, and negotiated claims of supremacy.

The word “coordination” matters. No single institution explains Tang success. The equal-field system could not supply revenue unless officials registered households. The fubing military system depended on local communities and exemptions from other duties. Frontier victories depended on Türk and other steppe soldiers as well as armies sent from China. Even Taizong’s reputation for good rule depended partly on advisers willing to criticize him. At the same time, coordination had limits. Tang armies could defeat a kingdom without making the conquered population accept Tang rule.

Check yourself: Choose one pair—land and taxes, households and soldiers, or victory and alliances—and explain why the two parts had to work together.

Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture, you will be able to…

  • Explain how the Tang foundation and Taizong’s 626 coup combined continuity with violence.
  • Connect household registration, equal-field land, taxes, fubing service, law, and official recruitment.
  • Compare Tang success against the Eastern Türks with its more limited results in Korea.

These objectives tell you what to do with the facts, not just what to memorize. The first asks you to explain a tension: the Tang inherited people and institutions from the Sui world, yet its own ruling family used violence to settle the succession. The second asks you to build a system. You should be able to draw arrows among registered households, land, grain and cloth taxes, labor, and military service. Law and official recruitment helped the court supervise that system. The third asks you to compare two frontiers. In 630 the Tang turned the collapse of the Eastern Türk qaghanate into a new claim of steppe leadership. In Korea, victories in 660 and 668 were followed by war with the former ally Silla and a retreat from most of the peninsula by 676.

Notice the verbs: explain requires causes, connect requires relationships, and compare requires both a similarity and a difference. The final activity asks you to use all three skills. If a term seems unfamiliar, first try to infer it from the slide, then use the popup or the key-term slide.

Check yourself: Which objective asks you to move beyond a list and describe a system with interacting parts?

Founding the dynasty

The Tang founders came from the same northwestern ruling world as the Sui.

  • Li Yuan was a Sui governor and member of the Guanlong elite.
  • He took Chang’an in 617 and founded the Tang in 618 as Sui rule collapsed.
  • The Li and Yang ruling houses were linked by marriage and shared military networks.
A new dynasty took over an existing imperial center, ruling class, and administrative inheritance.

Sources: Denis Twitchett, ed., Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; David A. Graff, Medieval Chinese Warfare; Digital Dunhuang, Cave 220.

×

Guanlong elite

A network of military families rooted around the passes (guan) near Chang’an and the Long region to the west. Many had served the Western Wei, Northern Zhou, and Sui. “Elite” here means families with offices, land, marriage connections, and military commands—not a single ethnic group or a modern political party.

The Tang founders did not arrive from outside the imperial system. Li Yuan had served the Sui as governor at Taiyuan. His family belonged to the Guanlong elite, a network of military and officeholding families centered around the Chang’an region and the northwest. These families had served several northern dynasties, including the Northern Zhou and Sui, and were connected by marriages. Li Yuan’s mother and the Sui emperor Wendi’s empress were sisters, so the Tang and Sui ruling houses were close relatives.

That continuity gave Li Yuan important advantages: experience, troops, allies, and knowledge of how the Sui state worked. In 617 he seized Chang’an and placed a young Sui prince on the throne. In 618, after Emperor Yangdi was killed elsewhere, Li Yuan removed that prince and declared the Tang. The mural is from 642 and shows an imperial figure in a Buddhist story. It is traditionally identified as Taizong, but it is not a portrait made simply to record his appearance. Read it as evidence for how early Tang artists pictured imperial authority surrounded by officials.

Check yourself: What two kinds of continuity helped the Tang founders take over the Sui state quickly?

Consolidation · 618–628

Founding the Tang in 618 did not mean controlling China in 618.

618Li Yuan becomes Emperor Gaozu at Chang’an.
621Li Shimin defeats Wang Shichong and Dou Jiande near Luoyang.
624Major southern rivals are defeated.
628The last major holdout, Liang Shidu, falls.
The Tang was founded by proclamation, but reunification required another decade of war and bargaining.

Sources: David A. Graff, Medieval Chinese Warfare; Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

A dynasty can announce its beginning in a day, but it cannot make every rival disappear by announcement. When Gaozu founded the Tang in 618, other warlords and regional regimes controlled much of the former Sui empire. Li Shimin, Gaozu’s second son, became the dynasty’s most important battlefield commander. In 621 he defeated Wang Shichong and Dou Jiande in the struggle for Luoyang and the eastern plain. Tang forces then continued south and northwest. By 624 most large southern rivals had fallen, but Liang Shidu held out in the north until 628.

This longer timeline corrects a common shortcut: “the Tang reunified China in 618.” The year 618 marks the dynasty’s foundation, not the completion of conquest. Tang victory also depended on absorbing surrendered soldiers and officials, confirming local leaders, and using the administrative routines already in place. Force mattered, but so did the ability to turn former enemies into subjects and servants of the new court. This pattern will return on the steppe after 630.

Why this matters: political control is a process. A capital, a dynastic name, and an emperor are not the same as effective rule across an empire.

Check yourself: Why is 628 a better endpoint for Tang military consolidation than 618?

Political memory in stone

Taizong made military service part of the dynasty’s founding story.

  • Saluzi carried Li Shimin during the 621 struggle near Luoyang.
  • The relief honors the horse and the general who saved it.
  • Made years later, it turns a dangerous battle into a story of loyalty and victory.
Commemoration tells us how rulers wanted the past remembered; it is not a battlefield photograph.

Source: Penn Museum, object C395; inscription and object history summarized by the museum.

This relief gives you a material source for Tang political memory. Saluzi, or “Autumn Dew,” was one of six horses honored at Taizong’s tomb complex, Zhaoling. During the fighting near Luoyang in 621, the horse was struck by an arrow. The figure beside it is General Qiu Xinggong, shown pulling the arrow from its chest. Taizong later ordered six stone reliefs to commemorate horses associated with his victories before he became emperor.

Look closely at the relationship between human and animal. The general is not shown conquering an enemy. Instead, he carefully tends the wounded horse. That choice turns war into a story about courage, loyal service, and mutual dependence. It also places Li Shimin’s military career at the center of the dynasty’s founding memory. The relief was made between 636 and 649, long after the battle, so it should not be treated as a direct record of what the scene looked like. It is a designed monument with a political purpose.

Why this matters: early Tang authority was built with armies, but later art gave that violence an honorable and emotionally powerful form.

Check yourself: What can this relief reliably tell you about 621, and what can it tell you more directly about Taizong’s later image?

Xuanwu Gate · 626

Li Shimin seized the throne through a family coup.

2 July 626Li Shimin ambushes Crown Prince Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji at Xuanwu Gate.
AfterwardThe two brothers’ sons are killed and Li Shimin becomes heir.
4 Sept. 626Gaozu abdicates; Li Shimin becomes Emperor Taizong.
The celebrated “Reign of Good Government” began with political murder and a forced change of succession.

Sources: Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; Howard J. Wechsler, Mirror to the Son of Heaven.

Li Shimin’s military success made him powerful, but it did not make him the official heir. His older brother Li Jiancheng held that position. Competition between the brothers’ followers became dangerous. On 2 July 626, Li Shimin and his men ambushed Li Jiancheng and a younger brother, Li Yuanji, at the northern gate of the palace complex, Xuanwu Gate. Both brothers were killed. Their sons were then executed, removing possible rivals from the next generation. Li Shimin became crown prince, and about two months later Gaozu abdicated. Li Shimin took the throne as Emperor Taizong.

Later court histories had strong reasons to justify Taizong’s action. They often portray Li Jiancheng as dangerous or unworthy and Li Shimin as the necessary savior of the dynasty. Historians must therefore separate the basic events from the moral explanation offered by sources written under the victor’s court. Taizong did become an effective ruler, but later success does not make his path to power peaceful or inevitable.

Why this matters: the early Tang combined impressive administration with coercion at the center. Both belong in the same story.

Check yourself: How does the Xuanwu Gate coup complicate the image created by the Saluzi relief?

Primary source · court criticism

Taizong later praised an adviser who told him when he was wrong.

Why Wei Zheng mattered

He had served Li Jiancheng, then became a forceful critic inside Taizong’s court.

What the quote claims

A ruler needs history and honest advisers to see mistakes that power can hide.

Wei Zheng makes the change from coup to government especially clear. Before 626, he had served Crown Prince Li Jiancheng and had reportedly urged him to act against Li Shimin. After the Xuanwu Gate coup, Taizong did not execute Wei Zheng. He brought him into the new government, where Wei became famous for direct criticism. When Wei died in 643, Taizong used the “three mirrors” comparison on this slide.

Read the source carefully. Bronze shows outward appearance. History shows patterns of rise and decline. A candid person shows a ruler’s current mistakes. The statement praises criticism, but it also helps Taizong present himself as the kind of emperor wise enough to accept criticism. The surviving account comes from the Old Book of Tang, compiled in the tenth century from earlier records. It preserves an influential court memory, not an audio recording. Taizong sometimes rejected advice, became angry with critics, or reversed policies, so the quote should be read as an ideal of government rather than proof that the ideal was always followed.

Check yourself: Why might accepting a former rival’s adviser strengthen a ruler after a violent coup?

Check yourself · court and consolidation

Which statement best explains early Tang continuity?

  1. The Tang rejected Sui officials and institutions to begin again.
  2. The Tang inherited elite networks and state structures, then consolidated them through war and political choices.
  3. The Tang controlled all of China immediately when Gaozu declared the dynasty in 618.
  4. Taizong’s good reputation proves that the 626 succession was peaceful.

Reveal the answer after choosing one.

×

Answer: B

The Tang founders came from the Sui governing world and inherited its capital and institutions, but they still needed about a decade of war to defeat rivals. Taizong’s 626 coup also shows that consolidation depended on coercive political choices.

Pause before opening the answer and explain your choice aloud or in one sentence. The correct answer is B. The Tang founders were closely connected to the Sui ruling world. Li Yuan had been a Sui governor, the Li and Yang houses were related, and both belonged to overlapping northwestern military networks. The Tang also inherited Chang’an, Sui administrative forms, and a reunified territorial ideal. Yet inheritance did not make power automatic. Rival regimes remained after 618, and Tang armies fought through the 620s. Inside the ruling family, the Xuanwu Gate coup settled the succession by killing Li Shimin’s brothers and their sons.

Option A is wrong because Tang rulers used and modified earlier institutions. Option C confuses the declaration of a dynasty with effective rule; the last major holdout did not fall until 628. Option D turns Taizong’s later reputation into a false description of how he took power. Historical evaluation requires you to keep effective government and political violence in view at the same time.

Study tip: when a claim uses words such as “all,” “immediately,” or “proves,” check whether it erases a complicated process.

Check yourself: Give one example of continuity and one example of coercion in the Tang consolidation.

Law

The Tang Code turned inherited law into a durable framework.

624First Tang code issued under Gaozu.
637Taizong-era revision reduces some severe penalties.
653Authoritative commentary issued under Gaozong.
LaterRevisions continue; the transmitted text includes later changes.
It is the earliest Chinese penal code preserved in full—not China’s first law code.

Sources: A. F. P. Hulsewé in Cambridge History of China, vol. 1; Wallace Johnson, trans., The T’ang Code; Shiga Shūzō, “A Basic History of T’ang Legislative Forms.”

The Tang Code grew from a long legal tradition. The Sui had already produced a code based on earlier northern models. Gaozu’s government issued a Tang code in 624, and Taizong’s court revised it in 637. Another version was issued under Gaozong in 651–652, followed by an authoritative commentary in 653. The commentary explained how short legal articles should be understood and applied. Revisions continued, and the complete text transmitted to later centuries includes changes from the early eighth century.

That last point keeps the claim accurate. Historians often call the Tang Code of 653 the earliest surviving complete Chinese code. This does not mean earlier dynasties lacked written law; much earlier legal texts survive in fragments, quotations, and excavated documents. It means the Tang penal code is the earliest one preserved as a complete system. It became a reference for later Chinese dynasties and for law codes in Korea, Japan, and Vietnam.

Why this matters: a code helped make decisions more consistent across time and distance, but it also expressed hierarchy. The same act could carry different consequences depending on family and status relationships.

Check yourself: What is the difference between “earliest law code” and “earliest law code preserved in full”?

The institutional core

Household registration connected people to the early Tang state.

Register
record household members, ages, and status
→
Assign duties
land, grain, cloth, labor, and military eligibility
→
Collect and mobilize
officials call for goods, workers, or soldiers
Registration did not simply count people. It made households visible for taxation and service.

The systems on the next slides all begin with registration. Local officials tried to record who belonged to each household, including age, sex, and legal status. Those records helped determine who could receive certain state land assignments and who owed grain, cloth, labor, or military service. Registers were therefore not neutral lists. They were tools that connected ordinary households to the demands of the state.

The system worked imperfectly. Officials could make errors, powerful families could hide dependents, and people could move or avoid registration. The court did not have equal administrative reach in every region. The equal-field system was strongest in areas where the state controlled land and kept detailed records, especially in the north; it was harder to enforce in parts of the south where patterns of landholding differed. Census totals therefore measure registered people, not every person who lived in the empire.

Why this matters: “state capacity” means more than having a strong emperor. It includes the ability to gather information and use it repeatedly. Registration let the Tang turn a broad claim to rule into specific obligations for particular households.

Check yourself: If a household disappeared from the register, which three kinds of resources might the state lose?

Land and taxes

Equal-field assignments supported a grain–labor–cloth tax system.

PartPlain-language meaningConnection to the state
Equal-fieldEligible registered people received use of specified state lands; rules varied by status and region.Land assignments tied cultivation to registration.
ZuAnnual grain payment.Fed the court, officials, and armies.
YongLabor service, often commuted into cloth.Supplied work or a substitute payment.
DiaoTextile or other local-product payment.Moved portable value to the state.

Sources: Wang Binghua and Helen Wang, “Tang Dynasty Tax Textiles”; Valerie Hansen, The Open Empire; Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

The phrase “equal-field system” can be misleading if you imagine the government repeatedly dividing every acre into equal private farms. The state assigned the use of particular lands according to rules based on registered people, age, and status. Some land returned to the state when the recipient died or became too old to qualify; other land could remain with a household. Private estates also existed. Implementation differed across regions and was especially difficult where the state did not control much land.

The early Tang tax system is often called zu-yong-diao. Zu was a grain payment. Yong was labor service, which could be replaced with a cloth payment. Diao was a payment in textiles or another approved product. These duties rested heavily on registered adult males, but textile production drew on women’s household labor. The system linked farming and weaving to the state without requiring every payment in coins.

Why this matters: land policy was not only about fairness. It supported a fiscal system: land helped households produce, while registers told officials what the households owed. The same connection could stabilize rule and impose heavy burdens.

Check yourself: Which part of zu-yong-diao could be paid either as work or, in many cases, as cloth?

Military organization

The fubing system used part-time soldiers rooted in local communities.

At home

Selected men farmed and trained in designated prefectures.

On rotation

Units supplied short guard tours at the capital.

On campaign

Troops joined temporary armies, then returned home when the campaign ended.

The system was concentrated in the northwest, and fubing were not the Tang’s only soldiers.

Source: David A. Graff, “The Reach of the Military: Tang,” Journal of Chinese History 1 (2017).

The fubing system organized part-time soldiers through several hundred local regimental headquarters. Men were selected partly for strength, household resources, and the number of adult males in the family. When not serving, they lived in their home communities, farmed, and trained. Units supplied rotating guard duty at the capital. During a war, the court created an expeditionary army under an appointed general; when the campaign ended, the soldiers and commander were supposed to return home. In exchange for full or partial tax exemptions, fubing usually provided much of their own equipment and supplies.

Two qualifications matter. First, regiments were distributed very unevenly: most were concentrated around Chang’an and across the northwest, reflecting the dynasty’s origins and security concerns. Second, the Tang also used temporary conscripts, frontier defense troops, professional guards, and large numbers of allied steppe soldiers. “The Tang army” was never one uniform organization.

Why this matters: fubing reduced the need for a permanent nationwide payroll and limited a general’s independent control by dissolving field armies after campaigns. But it depended on farms, households, and short wars. Long frontier deployments would eventually strain it.

Check yourself: Why did the fubing system work better for temporary campaigns than for permanent distant garrisons?

Recruiting officials

Schools and examinations created a route into office—but not an equal one.

  • Government schools taught classical texts and prepared a small pool of candidates.
  • Local recommendation, family privilege, and service connections still filled many posts.
  • Examination success could speed a career, especially for men already connected to elite culture.

Two important categories

Mingjing: close knowledge of the Confucian classics.

Jinshi: literary composition and questions about government; poetry gained importance later in the seventh century.

Sources: Cambridge History of China, vols. 3 and 5; Chen et al., The Political Economy of China’s Imperial Examination System (Cambridge, 2025).

The Tang expanded schools and examinations, but the early system was much smaller and less socially open than the later examination system you may know from the Song, Ming, or Qing. Government schools prepared sons of officials and some other young men. Candidates could enter examination categories such as mingjing, which stressed the Confucian classics, and jinshi, which tested literary composition and policy knowledge. Poetry became increasingly important to the jinshi examination later in the seventh century.

Passing did not automatically produce an office, and examinations were not the main route for every official. Family privilege, recommendations, school status, military service, and personal connections remained important. Recent scholarship emphasizes that the early Tang examinations did not immediately destroy the aristocracy. They often helped well-prepared members of elite families move quickly into high office. Still, they gave the central court another way to identify talent and helped define the knowledge officials were expected to share.

Why this matters: the examination route was both a change and a continuity. It widened competition somewhat, yet access to education and networks remained unequal. Lecture 3 will examine the elite more closely.

Check yourself: Why is “the Tang chose officials by examinations” true but incomplete?

Textual government

Standard texts helped officials study, argue, and govern from a shared reference point.

Classics
court-sponsored interpretations of Confucian texts
→
Schools and exams
students prepare from recognized works
→
Official histories
earlier dynasties become lessons for present rule
Standardization reduced disagreement about the base text; it did not eliminate debate about meaning.

Government depended on texts as well as taxes. Taizong’s court sponsored a major commentary on the Confucian classics under the scholar Kong Yingda. The project became known as the Correct Meaning of the Five Classics. It drew together earlier interpretations and provided an approved reference for state schools and examinations. The project was ordered under Taizong and completed in the following reign. Early Tang scholars also compiled official histories of several recent dynasties.

Standardization did not mean that every scholar agreed or that one book mechanically controlled every decision. It meant that students and officials could argue from a recognized textual foundation. The official histories performed another political task: they explained why earlier dynasties had risen and fallen. That made the past useful to present rulers. Taizong’s “three mirrors” saying expresses the same ideal—the past could reveal patterns and warn an emperor.

Why this matters: a large empire needs shared procedures and shared languages of authority. Codes standardized legal categories; registers standardized information about households; approved texts standardized part of elite learning. All three helped the court coordinate officials who served far from the emperor.

Check yourself: How did standard texts support both the examination system and the political use of history?

Check yourself · the institutional system

Put the pieces in a causal order.

Which sequence best explains how the early Tang converted households into state resources?

  1. Examinations → frontier conquest → household registration → land
  2. Household registration → land and duty assignments → taxes, labor, and eligible soldiers
  3. Law code → equal wealth → universal military service
  4. Fubing service → automatic examination success → official office

Reveal the answer after you explain your choice.

×

Answer: B

Registers identified households and eligible people. Officials then applied rules for land and obligations, which produced grain, cloth, labor, and military manpower. The system was uneven and imperfect, but that is the intended institutional chain.

The correct sequence is B. Household registration supplied the information on which other assignments depended. Once officials knew who belonged to a household and which people were eligible, they could apply rules for state land, grain and cloth payments, labor duties, and military selection. The chain did not work perfectly, and it was not equally strong everywhere, but it shows how the institutions were designed to fit together.

Option A begins with examinations, which recruited only a small portion of officials and did not create the household system. Option C is wrong because a legal code did not make wealth equal, and military service was not universal. Fubing selection was concentrated in particular regions and households, while the Tang also used other soldiers. Option D invents a direct link that did not exist: serving as a fubing did not automatically lead to passing a literary examination or receiving civil office.

Study tip: when you see an institutional question, draw arrows and label what moves along them—information, land, grain, cloth, labor, or people. That makes the system easier to remember than six separate definitions.

Check yourself: Name one point where this chain could break down and explain what resource the court would lose.

From the agrarian core to Inner Asia

Frontier power depended on relationships the court could not command in the same way.

The Tang combined armies with trade, titles, resettlement, alliances, and rule through local leaders.

The lecture now moves from institutions inside the registered agrarian core to political relationships across Inner Asia. The court could order a registered household to pay grain more directly than it could order a distant steppe ruler to obey. On the frontier, power depended on negotiation, coalition, and changing balances among many groups. Tang rulers used armies, but they also offered titles, trade, marriage ties, gifts, and official appointments. They resettled some defeated peoples and allowed other local leaders to retain authority under Tang recognition.

This does not create a simple contrast between “Chinese administration” and “foreign diplomacy.” Many Türk and other Inner Asian families lived inside Tang territory, served in Tang armies, or held Tang titles. Some Chinese officials negotiated on the steppe, while allied cavalry fought in Tang campaigns. The boundaries between internal and external rule were flexible.

Why this matters: maps often color an empire as a solid block. Early Tang influence was layered. Directly administered prefectures, military protectorates, allied states, and leaders who accepted titles could all appear within the same broad claim of supremacy, even though the court’s practical control differed greatly.

Check yourself: Why would a Tang title offered to a local ruler be useful even if the court did not directly administer that ruler’s people?

A frontier toolkit

Tang rulers used more than one method because frontier problems were not all alike.

Fight

Strike an enemy, defend a border, or remove a rival qaghan.

Negotiate

Exchange envoys, trade, gifts, hostages, titles, and marriage agreements.

Incorporate

Settle migrants, recruit allied troops, and recognize local chiefs as Tang officials.

The same group could be an enemy in one decade, an ally in the next, and a source of Tang soldiers throughout.

Sources: Jonathan Karam Skaff, Sui-Tang China and Its Turko-Mongol Neighbors; Shao-yun Yang, Early Tang China and the World.

This “toolkit” keeps frontier policy from becoming a list of battles. Fight includes defensive action, raids, and large campaigns. Negotiate includes envoys, regulated trade, gifts, titles, hostages, and marriage plans. These exchanges were political: they displayed rank, created obligations, and kept communication open. Incorporate means bringing people into Tang structures without necessarily making them identical to registered farming households in central China. The court could resettle groups, recruit their cavalry, or appoint a chief as a Tang prefect while allowing him to continue leading his own people.

The categories overlap. A military victory could create the conditions for negotiation. A defeated qaghan’s followers might then be resettled and recruited. An ally could later rebel, and an enemy’s prince could become a Tang general. The frontier was a political field of shifting relationships rather than a fixed line between two uniform civilizations.

Why this matters: Tang power was strongest when the court matched the tool to the situation and kept allies invested in the relationship. Direct conquest alone was often too expensive to maintain across great distances.

Check yourself: Which tool would best preserve a local leader’s authority while linking him to the Tang court?

Eastern Türks · 626–630

In four years, the Tang moved from danger at its capital to victory on the steppe.

626Eastern Türk forces reach the Wei River near Chang’an; Taizong negotiates their withdrawal.
627–629Harsh weather, rebellion, and rival steppe coalitions weaken the qaghanate.
630Li Jing’s campaign captures Illig Qaghan and breaks Eastern Türk power.
Tang victory exploited a steppe political crisis; it was not a contest between two isolated armies.

Sources: Shao-yun Yang, Early Tang China and the World; Skaff, Sui-Tang China and Its Turko-Mongol Neighbors.

Taizong’s steppe triumph was not inevitable. Only weeks after the Xuanwu Gate coup, Eastern Türk forces advanced to the Wei River near Chang’an in 626. Taizong negotiated their withdrawal and offered valuables. The event shows how exposed the new emperor was. The Tang founder Gaozu had earlier sought Türk support during the civil wars, so relations already included both dependence and rivalry.

Between 627 and 629, the Eastern Türk qaghanate suffered severe weather, internal revolts, and challenges from other steppe groups. Taizong’s court formed alliances with dissatisfied leaders. In 630, General Li Jing led a surprise winter campaign, captured Illig Qaghan, and shattered the qaghanate. Tang forces mattered, but the victory also depended on divisions and new coalitions within Inner Asia.

Why this matters: the rapid change from vulnerability in 626 to victory in 630 could encourage a simple story of Taizong’s genius. A better explanation combines leadership with timing, environmental pressure, and steppe politics. The Tang won by entering an existing struggle and building alliances as well as by fighting.

Check yourself: Name one internal Tang factor and one steppe factor that helped produce the victory of 630.

A hybrid claim to rule

Taizong became both Chinese emperor and Heavenly Qaghan.

Emperor

Son of Heaven ruling through dynastic institutions centered at Chang’an.

Heavenly Qaghan

A steppe title recognizing Taizong as superior ruler after the Eastern Türk collapse.

One ruler could speak in more than one political language.

Source: Shao-yun Yang, Early Tang China and the World, 618–750 CE (Cambridge, 2026), introduction.

×

Heavenly Qaghan · tian kehan

Qaghan was a supreme steppe ruler’s title, stronger than the ordinary English “khan.” In 630, rulers and envoys asked Taizong to accept the hybrid title tian kehan, often translated “Heavenly” or “Celestial Qaghan.” It claimed leadership over peoples once subordinate to the Eastern and Western Türk qaghans; it did not make every steppe community directly administered Tang territory.

After the victory of 630, assembled rulers and envoys asked Taizong to accept the title Heavenly Qaghan, or tian kehan. “Qaghan” was the title of a supreme steppe ruler; it is stronger and more precise here than the familiar word “khan.” “Heavenly” may echo the steppe concept of Tengri, the sky deity, while also sounding like the Chinese emperor’s title “Son of Heaven.” The result was a hybrid claim that could make sense in more than one political tradition.

The title did not mean that Taizong had turned all of Inner Asia into counties governed like the land around Chang’an. It meant that many rulers who had belonged to the Eastern or Western Türk political world now recognized his superior status. Taizong could confirm a local ruler’s successor and issue commands using both titles. Recognition depended on continuing power and relationships; it could disappear when those changed.

Why this matters: empires often rule different peoples through different languages of legitimacy. Taizong did not have to choose between being “Chinese” or “steppe.” His court claimed both forms of authority when each was useful.

Check yourself: Why is “Heavenly Qaghan” more informative than translating Taizong’s title simply as “Great Khan”?

Rule through local leaders

After 630, the Tang governed many steppe communities indirectly.

Defeat and submission
more than 100,000 Eastern Türk people accept Tang authority
→
Resettlement
communities placed in the Ordos and along the northern frontier
→
Bridle prefectures
chiefs receive Tang offices but keep local leadership
Indirect rule expanded Tang reach while limiting the cost of direct administration.

Source: David A. Graff, “The Reach of the Military: Tang”; Skaff, Sui-Tang China and Its Turko-Mongol Neighbors.

×

“Bridle” prefectures · jimi zhou

The Tang gave existing chiefs Chinese-style titles such as prefect or governor-general. They continued leading their own communities and could supply troops to Tang campaigns. The metaphor of a loose bridle suggests guidance without the same close control used in an ordinary prefecture.

The fall of the Eastern Türk qaghanate created a difficult question: what should the Tang do with the people who had followed it? More than 100,000 submitted and were settled in the Ordos region and other northern areas. Court officials debated whether they should live inside the frontier, be sent beyond the Yellow River, or be broken into smaller groups. The final arrangements changed over time because neither security nor loyalty was guaranteed.

One important tool was the bridle prefecture, or jimi zhou. The court gave a local chief a Chinese-style office such as prefect or governor-general. He continued to lead his own people, while recognizing the Tang emperor and supplying troops when called. This extended Tang influence without replacing every local custom or building a full Chinese bureaucracy. Steppe soldiers often served under their own leaders within larger Tang armies.

Why this matters: the arrangement was efficient but conditional. Tang titles could strengthen a chief, while the chief’s followers strengthened Tang campaigns. If either side no longer benefited, the relationship could break. Indirect rule therefore looks expansive on a map but was less secure than direct administration.

Check yourself: What did the Tang gain from a bridle prefecture, and what authority did a local chief keep?

The western regions

Tang armies and allies opened a chain of influence across the Tarim Basin.

640Gaochang conquered; a Tang prefecture established.
644Yanqi (Karashahr) attacked after changing allegiance.
648Kucha defeated; Tang influence reaches farther west.
657–658Western Türk qaghan defeated; Anxi Protectorate moved to Kucha.
This was a network of prefectures, protectorates, allied rulers, and contested routes—not one uniform block of direct rule.

Sources: Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; Shao-yun Yang, Early Tang China and the World.

The Tang expanded west in stages. Gaochang, an oasis kingdom near Turfan, was conquered in 640 and turned into a directly administered prefecture. Yanqi, also called Karashahr, changed its allegiance and was attacked in 644. Kucha fell in 648 after a campaign that included allied forces. Under Taizong’s successor Gaozong, Tang and allied armies defeated the Western Türk ruler Ashina Helu in 657, and the Anxi Protectorate was moved to Kucha in 658.

Do not imagine the entire area colored on a map as equally controlled. An ordinary prefecture had a different relationship to the court from a protectorate, an allied oasis king, or a steppe chief holding a Tang title. Garrisons protected routes and projected authority, but distance, supply, local politics, and competition from the Tibetan Empire made control unstable. Even a victory could require repeated campaigning.

Why this matters: “expansion” describes several relationships at once. The Tang could directly govern one oasis, supervise another through a protectorate, and claim supremacy over a distant ruler who still governed his own people. Recognizing those layers prevents the map from making empire look simpler than it was.

Check yourself: Which place on the timeline became a directly administered prefecture, and why should you not assume the same status for every other place?

Reading an empire map

A single boundary can hide several kinds of Tang authority.

  • The atlas maps Tang boundaries around 700, after the campaigns in this lecture.
  • Chang’an and the agrarian heartland were governed differently from protectorates in Central Asia.
  • Türk, Tibetan, Korean, and local oasis powers changed the meaning of the frontier over time.
Use the map to locate regions, not to assume equal control inside every line.

This historical atlas map helps you locate the Tang heartland, Mongolia, the Tarim Basin, and the Korean peninsula, but it needs careful reading. It shows boundaries around 700, about half a century after Taizong’s death. By then the Western Türk qaghanate had been defeated, the Tibetan Empire had become a major rival, and the political map had already changed several times. The map also comes from 1935, so its spellings and some interpretations reflect older scholarship.

The most important warning is about the boundary line. Inside it were directly governed prefectures, military protectorates, oasis kingdoms, and steppe communities led by their own chiefs. The court’s ability to collect taxes, appoint officials, and enforce orders differed across those spaces. Some areas might accept Tang titles when the empire was strong and reject them when another power offered better terms.

Why this matters: maps turn complicated political relationships into a clean visual shape. They are useful, but the shape is an argument. Pair the map with the terms “protectorate,” “bridle prefecture,” and “alliance” so that you do not mistake influence for uniform administration.

Check yourself: What question should you ask before treating any shaded frontier area as ordinary Tang territory?

Goguryeo · 644–645

Taizong prepared in 644, invaded in 645, and failed to take Ansi.

644Taizong orders preparations for war.
Spring 645Tang armies cross into Liaodong and take several fortresses.
Summer–autumnGoguryeo defenders hold Ansi fortress through a long siege.
Oct. 645Tang army retreats before winter with supply lines stretched.
The campaign won battles and captured forts, but it did not conquer Goguryeo.

Sources: Graff, Medieval Chinese Warfare; Cambridge History of China, vol. 3.

The original version of this lecture dated Taizong’s invasion to 644. The more precise sequence is that he decided on war and began major preparations in 644, while the invasion itself crossed into Liaodong in 645. Tang forces captured several fortresses and defeated Goguryeo armies in the field. The campaign then stalled at Ansi fortress. Its defenders resisted repeated assaults, while the Tang army faced lengthening supply lines and the approach of winter. Taizong ordered a retreat in October.

This was not a repeat of the Sui disaster at the Salsu River. The Tang army withdrew in organized fashion, and its losses were far smaller than the traditional figures attached to Yangdi’s campaign. Yet the strategic goal—breaking Goguryeo and imposing Tang control—was not achieved. Later raids also failed to force a quick settlement during Taizong’s lifetime.

Why this matters: “victory” can operate at more than one level. An army may win tactical battles and still fail strategically if it cannot capture the key fortress, maintain supplies, or make the opponent submit. Ansi marks the limit of Taizong’s celebrated military record.

Check yourself: Why is “Taizong lost every battle in Korea” inaccurate, and why is “Taizong conquered Goguryeo” also inaccurate?

Alliance, conquest, and reversal

Tang and Silla destroyed two kingdoms, then fought each other over the result.

660Tang–Silla forces conquer Baekje.
668The alliance conquers Goguryeo.
670–676Silla fights Tang attempts to control former Baekje and Goguryeo lands.
676Tang moves the Andong Protectorate from Pyongyang to Liaodong.
By 676 Silla controlled most of the peninsula south of the Taedong River; Tang retained a position in Liaodong rather than the whole conquered region.

Sources: Cambridge History of China, vol. 3; Kim Jong-bok, “Liaodong as a Buffer Zone”; Korean History and Culture Committee, A New History of Korea.

Taizong did not conquer Goguryeo, but the next reign changed the balance. Tang and Silla first destroyed Baekje in 660. In 668 their combined forces captured Pyongyang and ended Goguryeo. Tang officials then tried to administer the conquered lands through commanderies and protectorates. Silla had expected territorial gains and did not accept Tang control of the whole peninsula. The former allies fought from 670 to 676.

By 676 Tang had moved the Andong Protectorate from Pyongyang to Liaodong, northeast of the peninsula. Silla controlled most territory south of the Taedong River, though some northwestern areas remained a changing buffer. The Tang did not simply lose every trace of the earlier conquest: it retained influence and a position in Liaodong. But it failed to convert the joint victory of 668 into lasting rule over the peninsula.

Why this matters: alliances contain different goals. Tang and Silla agreed on defeating Baekje and Goguryeo; they did not agree on who would control the conquered lands. Once the shared enemies disappeared, that disagreement produced war.

Check yourself: What changed between the Tang–Silla alliance of 668 and the Tang–Silla conflict that followed?

Map · wars in Korea

The geography made conquest and supply different problems.

  • Liaodong’s fortified corridor guarded the approach from Tang territory.
  • Naval routes could move troops toward Baekje and Pyongyang.
  • Silla’s position in the southeast made it an essential ally—and later a powerful rival.
Distance, forts, rivers, seas, and allies shaped what armies could hold after they won.

Use this map to connect strategy to geography. Goguryeo controlled a broad area from northern Korea into Manchuria. Tang armies approaching overland had to cross the Liao River and pass a chain of fortified places in Liaodong. Ansi stood within that defensive zone. A fort did not have to defeat the entire invader; it could delay the army until supplies ran short and winter approached.

Later campaigns used both land and sea routes. Tang naval forces could move toward Baekje in the southwest or support operations near Pyongyang. Silla’s base in the southeast placed its forces on the peninsula and made the alliance indispensable. That same position mattered when Silla turned against Tang garrisons after 668. The ally that helped make conquest possible also helped prevent the Tang from keeping the whole result.

The arrows are schematic. They simplify several years of movement and should not be read as exact marching paths. Still, they make the central lesson visible: the farther an army moved from its supply bases, the more it depended on ships, fortified routes, local provisions, and allies.

Check yourself: Which geographic obstacle best helps explain the 645 failure, and which geographic advantage made Silla crucial to later campaigns?

Check yourself · frontier outcomes

Why did victory in 630 produce a different result from victory in 668?

  1. The Tang used only diplomacy in 630 and only armies in 668.
  2. The Eastern Türks had no local leaders, while Korea had no allies.
  3. In 630 the Tang entered a steppe collapse and built indirect relationships; after 668 it tried to control lands also claimed by Silla.
  4. The Tang never won a battle in Korea.

Reveal the answer after choosing one.

×

Answer: C

The 630 victory followed internal crisis within the Eastern Türk qaghanate and was converted into titles, resettlement, alliances, and indirect rule. The 668 conquest depended on Silla, whose territorial goals conflicted with Tang plans; the allies then fought over the settlement.

The best answer is C. In 630 the Tang took advantage of internal crisis within the Eastern Türk qaghanate and worked with rival steppe leaders. After the victory, Taizong used a steppe title, resettlement, Tang appointments, and indirect rule through local chiefs. Those arrangements were unstable, but they connected many former Türk subjects to the Tang without requiring the court to administer every community as an ordinary prefecture.

The conquest of Goguryeo in 668 also depended on an alliance, but Silla had its own territorial goals. Tang plans to govern the former Baekje and Goguryeo lands threatened those goals. The shared enemies were gone, and the alliance broke into war. By 676 Silla held most of the peninsula south of the Taedong River, while Tang shifted its northeastern command to Liaodong.

Option A falsely separates diplomacy from war; the Tang used both in each region. Option B erases local leadership and reverses the importance of allies. Option D is simply false: Tang forces won many battles and helped destroy two kingdoms. The issue was durable control after victory.

Check yourself: State the difference in one sentence using both words “alliance” and “control.”

Synthesis

Early Tang strength came from making different kinds of power reinforce one another.

Information
register households and standardize texts and law
→
Resources
collect grain, cloth, labor, officials, and soldiers
→
Relationships
manage advisers, allies, chiefs, and conquered peoples
Durable rule required cooperation. Institutions made demands repeatable; relationships determined whether people carried them out.

This slide brings the lecture back to coordination. Information came from household registers, legal categories, approved classical texts, and official histories. Resources included grain and cloth taxes, labor service, trained officials, fubing rotations, other conscripts, and allied cavalry. Relationships connected the ruler to critical advisers, local elites, steppe chiefs, allied kingdoms, and the populations the Tang tried to govern.

The arrows should not be read as a one-way machine. Information was useless if officials could not collect resources. Resources were hard to collect if households hid, fled, or resisted. Frontier titles worked only while local leaders and followers found the Tang relationship valuable. Taizong’s relationship with Wei Zheng shows the same principle at court: an emperor needed information that only another person could provide, including criticism he might not want to hear.

Why this matters: “strong state” does not mean rulers can do anything. Strength comes from institutions that organize repeated action and from people willing or compelled to participate. The Korean wars show the limit: military victory could remove a kingdom without producing a political settlement acceptable to the former ally Silla.

Check yourself: Give one example from the lecture for each box—information, resources, and relationships.

Key terms

Nine terms that explain early Tang power

Gaozu · Taizong

First and second Tang emperors; father and son.

Xuanwu Gate

Site of Li Shimin’s 626 coup against his brothers.

Tang Code

Penal code revised across the seventh century; earliest complete Chinese code preserved.

Equal-field

Rules assigning use of certain state lands to registered people.

Zu-yong-diao

Grain, labor (or substitute), and textile obligations.

Fubing

Part-time soldiers organized in local regiments, concentrated in the northwest.

Heavenly Qaghan

Steppe title Taizong accepted after the 630 victory.

Bridle prefecture

Indirect rule through a local chief holding a Tang office.

Goguryeo · Silla

Kingdom conquered in 668; ally that then resisted Tang control.

Use these nine terms to retell the lecture rather than memorizing nine isolated definitions. Gaozu founded the Tang, and Taizong seized the succession at Xuanwu Gate. Inside the empire, the Tang Code provided a legal framework. The equal-field system linked registered people to certain land assignments, while zu-yong-diao named obligations in grain, labor or its substitute, and textiles. The fubing system organized selected part-time soldiers through local regiments, especially in the northwest.

Beyond the agrarian core, Taizong’s title Heavenly Qaghan claimed leadership in a steppe political language. A bridle prefecture linked a local chief to the Tang court without replacing his authority with ordinary direct administration. Finally, Goguryeo and Silla remind you that an ally can help destroy a rival and then reject the victor’s plans for the conquered land.

Study tip: sort the terms into court, institutions, and frontiers. Then identify the terms that connect two groups. Taizong, for example, belongs in all three.

Check yourself: Which term best shows indirect rule, and which term best shows the connection between households and taxation?

Five-minute writing activity · work on your own

Explain how early Tang institutions supported stability—and where they reached a limit.

How did the Tang structure military service, land and tax obligations, and civil-service recruitment to strengthen the state under rulers such as Taizong?

Write 4–6 sentences. Use one example each for military organization, land/taxation, and official recruitment. Then add one frontier example showing why victory did not always produce lasting control. End by deciding: which connection mattered most, and why?

Adapted from Review Question 2 in the course textbook, ch. 5.

This activity asks you to build an argument from the institutional system and then test it against a frontier example. Begin with a clear claim: early Tang stability came from linking registered households and educated officials to repeatable obligations. For military organization, you might use the fubing system—part-time soldiers trained locally, served capital rotations or temporary campaigns, and then returned home. For land and taxation, explain how equal-field assignments and household registers supported grain, cloth, and labor obligations. For civil service, describe schools and the mingjing or jinshi examinations while noting that family privilege and recommendations still mattered.

Your frontier example should add a limit, not cancel the first part. You could compare the 630 defeat of the Eastern Türks with indirect rule through chiefs, or explain how Tang and Silla conquered Goguryeo in 668 but fought over the settlement until 676. Finish by choosing the most important connection. A strong answer does not simply say “all were important”; it explains why one enabled the others—for example, registration supplied both revenue and military eligibility.

Check yourself: Does your answer include three institutions, one frontier limit, and a final judgment supported by a reason?
